claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can maintain single-phase compositional uniformity during reactive-atmosphere service up to approximately 1173 K.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% noble metal suppresses environment-driven surface segregation in these nanoparticles.
Minor noble-metal doping reduces differential diffusion rates among constituent elements.
Reduced differential diffusion inhibits depletion of constituent elements at the nanoparticle surface.
The starting nanoparticles are near-equiatomic transition-metal nanoparticles with minimal or zero noble-metal content and a predominantly single-phase solid-solution structure.
Half of the nanoparticles will receive a small Pt fraction while the other half will remain undoped.
Doped and undoped samples will be exposed to reactive gas at 1 bar and 973–1173 K for at least 24 hours.
The relevant structural mediator is surface segregation versus preservation of bulk-like short-range ordering.
The noble-metal dopant stabilizes the near-surface region.
Minor noble-metal doping modifies local defect energetics.
Modified defect energetics reduce preferential surface enrichment of more reactive species.
Reduced surface enrichment mitigates phase separation and compositional-gradient formation under reactive high-temperature conditions.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, doped nanoparticles will retain a more nearly equiatomic surface composition.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, doped nanoparticles will show delayed or negligible formation of secondary phases or segregated regions.
Relative to undoped nanoparticles, doped nanoparticles will preserve single-phase structural coherence for longer times or at higher temperatures.
Undoped nanoparticles will form transient or persistent surface-segregated phases and lose single-phase stability sooner under the same conditions.
The proposed dopant effect is strongest in moderately oxidative or reactive atmospheres between 773 and 1173 K.
Conditions outside the stated temperature or pressure range, or noble-metal doping above approximately 5 at.%, may change the governing mechanism or produce additional phases.
The doping threshold and its dependence on gas composition are not established.
A lack of significant difference between doped and undoped samples in both surface segregation and phase stability would falsify the proposed dopant-mediated suppression mechanism.
